<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) has shaped dementia care reforms and informed innovative long-term care models such as care villages. Recreational activities are often seen as a site where PCC is enacted, yet little empirical work has examined how participation in structured activities is enabled, mediated, and constrained through everyday social, relational, and organizational dynamics. This study examines how participation in structured group activities was produced in a care village.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An ethnographic study was conducted in Canada’s first publicly funded care village, drawing on 100 hours of participant observation, 12 staff interviews, and informal resident conversations. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participation varied across activity types and residents’ fluctuating comfort, stamina, and readiness. For many residents, participation was not simply an individual decision, but was scaffolded through staff invitation, accessible information, relational familiarity, and individualized encouragement. It also depended on logistical and organizational conditions, including preparation, transportation, staffing coordination, and role boundaries. These findings show that participation was relationally and organizationally produced rather than simply a matter of resident preference or program design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>

These insights have implications for staffing, coordination, and activity provision in care villages and long-term care settings.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To explore age-specific insights into how older adults understand and decide about health screening, using dementia screening as a critical case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 44 community-dwelling older adults in Singapore (ages 64–87). Six focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted. Audio recordings were transcribed, standardized into English, and verified through independent bilingual checks. Data were analyzed using a hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis grounded in Health Belief Model constructs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six main themes with twelve subthemes were identified from the analysis. Dementia understanding described participants’ general awareness of dementia and confusion between normal ageing and cognitive impairment. Risk perceptions included perceived severity and susceptibility, with many viewing dementia as an inevitable part of ageing rather than something preventable. Perceived benefits encompassed early detection, improved awareness, and protection of family members through future planning. Perceived barriers involved both practical and psychological factors, including financial cost, accessibility, fear of diagnosis, and concerns over autonomy loss. Perceived support highlighted the influence of family encouragement, community resources, and spiritual faith in motivating or discouraging screening decisions. An emergent theme of self-ageism reflected internalized beliefs that screening was unnecessary, inappropriate, or futile in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dementia screening, as a critical case, revealed how self-ageism, alongside conventional HBM constructs, shapes older adults’ screening intentions, underscoring the need for inclusive health communication for aging populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “Not for Our Age”: Self-Ageism in Older Adults’ Dementia Screening Decision

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gratitude and savoring have great potential to support well-being in older age, but most studies on positive psychology interventions have been conducted among healthy young adults. This narrative review explored gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults, with or without dementia, including (1) the characteristics of these interventions, (2) their acceptability for older users, and (3) their effect on mental health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scopus, PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched in December 2023 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined gratitude or savoring interventions among older adults. Multi-component intervention studies were excluded. Two researchers independently screened 2423 studies and assessed methodological quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Numerical and narrative data were extracted and synthesized regarding intervention characteristics, acceptability, and effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 11 included articles, five examined gratitude, five examined savoring, and one compared both. Only one study included participants with dementia. Adherence was generally high, suggesting a good fit, but participant evaluation was lacking. Four acceptability themes were highlighted concerning the target group, setting and delivery mode, dosage, and content and tailoring. Most studies showed improved well-being and reduced psychopathology, although not consistently on all outcome measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There is initial evidence that gratitude and savoring interventions could be suitable to promote mental health among older adults with relatively preserved cognitive function. Future research should examine the need for tailoring in terms of dose, delivery method and content, and applicability to more diverse groups of older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults: a narrative review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article explores the discursive, industrial, artistic, and practical interconnections between older people, aging, and holography, arguing that their nexus mutually shapes how both concepts are culturally constituted. Methodologically, the paper utilizes a discourse and representation analysis to examine a heterogeneous corpus of actual wave-optic holography and pseudo-holographic lens-optic phantasmagorias—collectively addressed as “(quasi-)holographic” phenomena. Dissolving the boundaries between cultural fiction and industrial technology, the analysis tracks two central thematic clusters revolving around exclusion and inclusion to interrogate how older adults are integrated into techno-social futures. The paper demonstrates that while older individuals are frequently subjected to exclusionary transhumanist logics or paternalistic, resource-scarcity-driven care practices, they also emerge as active agents of inclusive technology. By analyzing cases ranging from speculative science fiction to real-world care appliances, this study maps a neglected intersection in media and aging studies. Ultimately, it introduces the concept of “geronto-futurist” interventions. These practices not only expose the marginalized position of older adults in technological imaginations but actively reshape techno-futurities. By introducing an age lens to media practices, this article contributes to broader discussions of techno-social equality, highlighting how notions of later life actively shape contemporary understandings of digitality.</jats:p>
title: From ‘Old Man Yells at Cloud’ to Geronto-Futurism: Co-Imagining Holography and Aging

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cortisol dysregulation, reflective of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, has been linked to executive functioning (EF) decline. However, substantial effect-size heterogeneity across studies highlights the potential role of psychosocial moderators. We investigated whether the severity of perceived daily stressors and chronic worry moderated the relationships between baseline cortisol dysregulation and 9-year EF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community adults (N = 1,617) completed four-day, four-times-daily salivary cortisol sampling and an eight-day interview-driven daily diary at baseline. Three cortisol metrics were computed: area under the curve (AUC), cortisol awakening response (CAR), and diurnal cortisol slope (DCS). Linear mixed models determined whether daily stressor or chronic worry severity moderated associations between baseline cortisol metrics and 9-year EF, adjusting for baseline EF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daily stressor severity significantly moderated the relationship between DCS–but not AUC or CAR–and 9-year EF (Cohen’s d = 0.113). Flatter DCS was associated with poorer EF across all stressor severity levels, although the observed numerical attenuation at higher severity was not statistically confirmed. Chronic worry severity was significantly associated with lower 9-year EF across all cortisol metrics and significantly moderated the CAR-to-EF relationship (d = –0.176). Exploratory analyses suggested that a flatter DCS was associated with worse EF at higher worry severity, but this interaction was not significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These outcomes broadly align with moderation, not mediation, suggesting that psychosocial stress and worry can amplify, rather than yield, cortisol-linked relationships with EF. Pending replication, HPA-axis circadian modulation and chronic worry severity can indicate viable targets for prevention research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Blunted Diurnal Cortisol Slope as a Risk Marker for 9-Year Executive Function Decline: Amplification by Daily Stress and Worry Severity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Personality characteristics are recognized as early indicators of later cognitive functioning, yet existing studies have primarily focused on trait-level trends. How well these between-person differences uncover daily cognitive functioning processes remains unclear. Addressing this entails examining momentary personality states, which may accumulate over time to influence longer-term cognitive outcomes. Accordingly, this study investigates associations between personality traits and states and momentary cognitive functioning and variability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a three-week ecological momentary assessment study of middle-aged and older adults (N = 183). We used Bayesian Mixed-Effects Location Scale Models to capture contingencies between personality and momentary cognitive functioning/variability. Additionally, we used machine learning (elastic net regression) to identify profiles of personality state-cognition contingencies and individuals who exhibit stronger associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At the trait level, higher conscientiousness was associated with poorer working memory and processing speed. Higher openness was associated with better cognitive functioning and lower variability for episodic memory and processing speed. At the state level, conscientiousness was associated with better working memory performance, while neuroticism was associated with variable episodic memory functioning. Extraversion was associated with working and episodic memory functioning/variability. Finally, sociodemographic, health, and personality trait variables emerged as top predictors of individual differences in within-person associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By investigating within-person associations between personality and cognitive ability, we demonstrate that trait-level associations do not necessarily generalize to state-level ones. Profiles of top predictors of individual differences in state-level associations may be promising targets for intervention, but interventions should be tailored with between- and within-person differences in mind.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Personality trait and state associations with cognitive functioning and variability in middle-aged and older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Self-rated memory impairment is common in older age and has been related to objective cognitive decline and dementia. Recently, there has been growing interest in early-life predictors of late-life cognition, but research has been limited due to the absence of data spanning the entire lifespan. The present study investigated whether psychological health, social well-being, socioeconomic status (SES), and cognitive abilities at age 10 and 13 predicted subjective memory almost six decades later.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychological health, social well-being, SES, and cognitive abilities were measured with standardized tests and questionnaires at age 10 and 13. Subjective memory, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured with the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (PRMQ) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at age 67 (n = 625).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a longitudinal autoregressive structural equation model (SEM), higher levels of psychological health at age 13 predicted lower levels of subjective memory at age 67. This association was independent of current anxiety and depressive symptoms. The model did not provide sufficient support that social well-being, SES, cognitive ability, and school performance at age 13 predicted subjective memory at age 67. Additional analysis revealed that psychological health at age 13, but not at age 10, and anxiety symptoms at age 67 uniquely predicted subjective memory at age 67.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend prior research by showing that psychological health is a robust predictor of subjective memory. Interventions targeting early-life psychological health may help identify individuals with different prospective cognitive outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A growing body of literature suggests that self- or patient- reported health may be associated with objective health outcomes. Self-reported health could thus be a non-invasive and low-cost way of identifying who is at risk of poor health in later life. However, no prior study has systematically examined this relationship using multiple large datasets. The goal of the current study was thus to examine the extent to which self-rated health was associated with cognitive function, a distinct outcome rather than an aspect of health itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a coordinated data analysis (CDA) methodological framework, we identified 15 longitudinal datasets comprising over 140,000 participants representing 38 countries that met our analytic inclusion criteria. Our preregistered analyses tested 1) whether self-rated health was associated with cognitive function both concurrently and at longitudinal follow-up, 2) the odds of developing cognitive impairment or dementia over the course of the study, and 3) whether these associations persisted net of demographic and health covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across nearly all datasets, higher self-rated health was associated with better cognitive function (both concurrently and longitudinally) and lower odds of developing dementia, over and above the effects of chronic conditions. Age moderated some effects, such that these associations may be strongest among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of the predictive utility of single-item subjective health indicators on downstream health outcomes and the benefits of using CDA in aging research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations between indicators of self-rated health, cognitive function, risk of cognitive impairment, and dementia: A coordinated data analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Menopause is a heterogeneous transition that varies in timing and type, yet population-based research rarely considers how reproductive life course experiences shape menopausal outcomes. This study examines whether reproductive timing, reproductive history, and reproductive health across adolescence and adulthood are associated with menopausal status, early menopause, and surgical menopause at midlife.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from women in Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we constructed reproductive life course histories including pubertal timing, pregnancy and parity, reproductive complications, and gynecologic conditions. Menopausal outcomes at Wave VI included menopausal status, early menopause (before age 40), and surgical menopause. Survey-weighted logistic regression models estimated associations between reproductive characteristics and menopausal outcomes, adjusting for socioeconomic context and cumulative reproductive stress. Stratified analyses by pregnancy history assessed whether associations with gynecologic pathology were independent of fertility history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At Wave VI (mean age 44), 18% of women were postmenopausal. Among them, 69% reported surgical menopause and 60% experienced menopause before age 40, indicating a substantial prevalence of non-natural and early transitions. Pregnancy and parity were consistently associated with menopausal outcomes, whereas reproductive timing showed more limited associations. Gynecologic pathology was strongly associated with early and surgical menopause independent of pregnancy history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Menopause emerges as a life course process shaped by reproductive histories and midlife reproductive health. The high prevalence of early and surgical menopause underscores the importance of examining heterogeneous pathways to menopausal timing and type in population-based research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Reproductive life course histories and menopausal outcomes at midlife: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lifestyle activity engagement in later life may protect against dementia, but studies have often been limited to short follow-up periods and predominantly White samples. We examined activity variety and frequency as predictors of incident dementia, leveraging 15 years of linked longitudinal insurance claims data in the Baltimore Experience Corps Study (BECS).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 482 individuals from BECS (2006-2013) with linked insurance claims (mean age=68.2, 84% women, 95% Black/African American). Participants self-reported baseline engagement in 28 activities. We calculated the number of unique activities (activity variety) and average frequency of engagement across reported activities (activity frequency). Incident dementia (2008-2022) was ascertained from CMS and private claims using the Bynum-EM algorithm. We used Cox proportional hazards models, adjusting for age and intervention group, and tested multiple follow-up periods (5-year, 15-year).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The average baseline variety was 18.8 activities (SD = 3.3) and frequency was 13.1 days/month (SD = 3.2). For the 15-year follow-up only, higher activity variety was associated with lower risk of incident dementia (HR=.94, 95% CI: 0.89-0.99), equivalent to about a 6-month delay in diagnosis per additional activity. This association was attenuated after adjusting for additional demographics (e.g., sex, education), prevalent health conditions, and depression (HR=.96, 95% CI: 0.90-1.01). Activity frequency was not significant in any model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher activity variety, but not frequency, modestly predicted lower dementia risk over 15 years in a sample of primarily Black older adults. Findings suggest that engagement in a range of activities, rather than more frequent engagement in limited activities, may elicit greater cognitive benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Lifestyle activities and risk of incident dementia from linked insurance claims in the Baltimore Experience Corps Study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Informal caregivers’ beliefs about caregiving for older adults (i.e. caregiver stigma) are associated with suicidal ideation and poor mental health. As only few studies have studied this association, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study analyzed whether caregiver stigma is associated with suicidal ideation and depression via feelings of entrapment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Canadian long-term caregivers of adults aged 60+ years (N = 175, 18-95+ years) were surveyed online with the internalized caregiver stigma scale (self-devaluing (negative) and self-affirming (positive) stereotypes, attitudes, and behaviors), about their feelings of entrapment (short entrapment scale), depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation (PHQ-9). Regression analysis with robust standard errors and causal mediation analysis with bootstrapped standard errors were conducted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Regression models indicated entrapment and negative care stigma were associated with more depressive symptoms, and entrapment with higher suicidal ideation. Significant indirect effects of positive and negative caregiver stigma components on suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms via entrapment were found in the causal mediation models. Additionally, positive caregiver stigma interacted with entrapment in the model for suicidal ideation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlighted that the path from negative caregiver self-stigma to a higher level of suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms seems to be rooted through increased feelings of entrapment. Conversely, the self-affirming form of caregiver stigma had a hidden protective effect for both outcomes via lower feelings of entrapment. Targeting care-related stigma may thus help reduce the danger of negative mental health outcomes among caregivers of older adults by changing their constricting perception of being trapped.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Seeing no way out: Exploring the connection between internalized caregiver stigma, entrapment, suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms among Canadian informal caregivers

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the Social Ecological Model (SEM), this study aimed to examine multilevel influences on social participation among community-dwelling older adults from the perspectives of older adults and community workers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. The quantitative component included 641 community-dwelling older adults from five communities in Beijing, China. The qualitative component involved semi-structured interviews with 18 older adults and 14 community workers. Findings were integrated through an SEM-guided joint display and triangulation protocol.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older age, cognitive impairment, impairment of activities of daily living, and poor self-rated health were associated with lower social participation, whereas higher educational attainment, social support, weekly exercise, and active community encouragement were associated with higher participation. Qualitative findings identified 10 subthemes, showing that participation was also linked to interest preferences, family and peer relationships, communication and mobilization, activity design, accessibility, resource support, and policy and institutional conditions. Integrated analysis showed the clearest convergence for health- and function-related influences, while qualitative findings clarified how social support and community encouragement operated in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social participation among community-dwelling older adults appears to be associated with interrelated factors across individual, interpersonal, community, and societal levels. Efforts to support participation in later life may benefit from addressing not only functional vulnerability but also the relational, organizational, and contextual conditions that makes participation feasible in community settings.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Advance care planning (ACP) is increasingly conceptualized as a proactive, communication-centered process that supports person-centered care in later life. Although prior research has focused on demographic and clinical predictors, less is known about the psychological factors that shape how individuals engage in planning. Guided by Stereotype Embodiment Theory, this study examined whether self-perceptions of aging (SPA) prospectively predict patterns of ACP engagement.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from the Health and Retirement Study (2008–2014). ACP was categorized as: both formal (documentation) and informal (discussion) planning, formal-only, informal-only, or neither. Multinomial logistic regression models assessed associations between SPA and ACP patterns, adjusting for sociodemographic and health characteristics. Interaction models tested moderation by sociodemographic and health factors, and exploratory analyses examined transitions into ACP among baseline nonplanners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More positive baseline SPA was associated with a lower likelihood of engaging in formal-only ACP relative to engaging in both formal and informal ACP. SPA was not significantly associated with informal-only ACP or with no ACP relative to comprehensive planning. Associations between SPA and ACP patterns did not vary across sociodemographic groups, although functional limitations and self-rated health modestly moderated specific contrasts. Among respondents with no prior ACP, SPA did not significantly predict transitions into planning over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend Stereotype Embodiment Theory to future-oriented healthcare planning and highlight SPA as a psychosocial factor associated with comprehensive ACP engagement.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings indicate that the loss of higher SNAP benefits substantially increased food hardship among low-income older adults post-COVID, underscoring the need for adequate benefit levels.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Health shocks may reshape health behaviors in later life, yet their implications for dietary habits remain insufficiently understood. Using six waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey from 2002 to 2018, this study examines the association between serious illness episodes and dietary diversity among Chinese older adults. The results show that health shocks are significantly associated with lower dietary diversity. This association remains stable across sensitivity analyses. Heterogeneity analyses further indicate that the negative association is stronger among the oldest adults and those with a higher chronic disease burden. Mechanism analyses suggest that financial condition, physiological functioning, and outdoor activity partly account for the association. These findings suggest that, among older adults in China, health shocks may operate more as constraints that reduce the capacity to maintain diverse diets. Post-illness care should therefore integrate nutritional support, functional recovery, and community-based assistance, especially for older adults with greater health vulnerability.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Caring for a parent with dementia constitutes a profound relational and existential transition for adult children, extending beyond functional caregiving demands to processes of identity negotiation and reconstruction. Although extensive research has documented caregiver burden, psychological distress, and health consequences in dementia caregiving, comparatively little attention has been devoted to the narrative mechanisms through which caregivers sustain a coherent sense of self. Drawing on narrative identity theory, ambiguous loss theory, and the concept of biographical disruption, this qualitative narrative study explored how adult children construct identity narratives while caring for a parent with dementia. Semi-structured narrative interviews with 21 caregivers were analyzed using a holistic narrative approach informed by narrative selection theory. Four dominant narrative identity patterns emerged: management narratives emphasizing control and competence, growth narratives framing caregiving as personal transformation, protective boundary narratives focusing on identity differentiation, and fracture and alienation narratives. These narratives functioned as adaptive mechanisms for negotiating agencies, continuity, and moral positioning under conditions of chronic relational loss. The findings extend dementia caregiving research by conceptualizing caregiving as an ongoing narrative identity project rather than solely a burden experience, highlighting the central role of meaning-making, cultural expectations, and epistemic agency in caregiver adaptation.</jats:p>
title: Reconstructing Identity in the Shadow of Dementia: Narrative Identity Processes Among Adult Child Caregivers

records.abstract: <jats:p>Health-related quality of life reflects individuals’ perceptions of how a health condition affects their physical, psychological, and social functioning. Amid increasing pressures on primary care systems, people living with dementia are presenting more frequently to hospital settings. However, limited research has explored how hospital-based care, and the dementia stigma that may operate within it, shapes health-related quality of life for people living with dementia and their caregivers. This exploratory qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with 15 participants, including people living with dementia and caregivers of individuals who had attended an emergency department or been hospitalized in Canada within the past two years. The interview guide was informed by the Wilson and Cleary Model of Health-related Quality of Life and intentionally avoided terms such as “stigma,” “bias,” or “discrimination” to reduce response priming. Data were analyzed using Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis and mapped to health-related quality of life factors (i.e., characteristics of the individual, biological and physiological factors, general health perceptions, etc.). Twelve caregivers (mean age 59.8 years, standard deviation = 9.7) and three people living with dementia (mean age 70.6 years, standard deviation = 11.8) participated between September and December 2025. Five interrelated discourses emerged: (1) characteristics of the individual: identity precedes clinical assessment; (2) biological and physiological factors: dementia disclosure as double-edged; (3) symptom and functional status: diagnostic overshadowing; (4) general health perceptions: equating dementia to futility; and (5) characteristics of the environment: structural barriers to recovery. Hospital-based discourses that implicitly or explicitly associate dementia with decline and therapeutic futility may contribute to stigma and negatively influence health-related quality of life for people living with dementia, while also intensifying caregiver distress. These findings underscore the need for stigma-reduction strategies in acute care settings that challenge therapeutic nihilism (i.e., inappropriately pessimistic view of patient outcomes) and promote person-centered, equitable hospital care.</jats:p>
title: “You Don’t Belong in Hospital”: How Hospital-Based Dementia Stigma Shapes Health-Related Quality of Life

<jats:p>
                    South Texas has among the highest dementia prevalence rates in the United States, yet communities in the region remain consistently underrepresented in dementia research. Aligning research studies with what matters to communities most impacted by dementia is critical in addressing the crisis of research exclusion. This participatory study sought to identify community-driven dementia research priorities grounded in the experiences and needs of South Texas residents impacted by dementia. A two-year community-engaged study was conducted in partnership with a Community Council composed of individuals living with dementia, family caregivers, community health workers, and community-serving professionals. A plática program model was co-developed and implemented to elicit lived experiences with dementia and inform the development of a priority-setting survey. The resulting survey included 21 research topics grouped into four themes: (1) awareness of dementia, (2) experiences living with dementia, (3) families caring for someone living with dementia, and (4) resources to support families. Respondents (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                    = 152) rated each topic on a 1–10 importance scale and selected their top two priorities by theme. Descriptive statistics were used to identify highly rated and frequently prioritized topics. Importance ratings were uniformly high across all topics (range: 8.44–9.39). Ranking data revealed clear priorities within themes wherein respondents prioritized timely diagnosis, improved provider communication, behavioral symptom management using non-pharmacological approaches, co-caregiving strategies, and system-level resources such as financial and legal planning supports. These priorities were largely consistent across respondent subgroups. The participatory approach of this study enhances the relevance of findings and demonstrates the value of community-engaged methods for shaping research agendas. These community-defined priorities offer timely direction for researchers, funders, and policymakers aiming to reduce dementia disparities in South Texas and improve the equity, translational potential, and impact of future research.
                  </jats:p>
title: Studying What Matters: South Texas Community-Driven Dementia Research Priorities

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Telomere length (TL) is a well-established biomarker of cellular senescence, yet the metabolic profile of TL and its associations with aging-related phenotypes and responses to modifiable lifestyle factors remain unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TL was measured using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in 282 participants from the West China Health and Aging Cohort (WCHAC). Plasma metabolites were analyzed using Liquid Chromatography-tandem Mass Spectrometry. TL-associated metabolic signatures (Met-TL) were identified through elastic net regression models. Associations between Met-TL and aging-related phenotypes and modifiable lifestyle factors were evaluated using linear and logistic regression models in a larger, non-overlapping sample of 5,957 WCHAC participants. Furthermore, we employed mediation analysis to explore the mediating effects of Met-TL between lifestyle factors and aging-related diseases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified a plasma metabolite signature comprising 26 metabolites explaining 17.5% of TL variance. Met-TL significantly associated with aging-related phenotypes (44 Bonferroni-corrected associations) and modifiable lifestyle factors (4 associations). Notably, Met-TL showed robust associations with steatohepatitis and hepatic biomarkers. Mediation analysis revealed that Met-TL partially explained the protective association between healthy lifestyle and steatohepatitis, with a mediation proportion of 8.2%.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings provide novel insights into the metabolic profile of TL in older adults. The Met-TL may serve as a promising biomarker of cellular aging, particularly in identifying liver dysfunction, facilitating the development of personalized aging monitoring and anti-aging intervention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Metabolomic Profiling of Telomere Length: Associations with Aging-related Phenotypes and Modifiable Lifestyle Factors in Chinese Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Epigenetic clocks have emerged as markers of biological aging. Understanding their association with age-related functional decline may provide insights into DNA-mediated mechanisms underlying frailty-related functional decline and reveal which clocks best associate with accelerated functional decline. We therefore examined associations between established epigenetic clock measures and longitudinal trajectories of cognitive function, grip strength, and walking speed. We analyzed data from 4,018 participants in the Health and Retirement Study with available DNA methylation data and up to 12 years of follow-up data. Using linear mixed-effects models, we examined retrospective associations between twelve epigenetic clocks and longitudinal trajectories of frailty-related functional decline, modeling interactions between each epigenetic clock and time, adjusting for chronological age and sociodemographic covariates. In longitudinal analyses controlling for chronological age, older epigenetic age was associated with faster cognitive decline for Hannum (β = -0.0054, 95% CI: -0.0095, -0.0014, p = 0.009) and DNAmGrimAge (β = -0.0141, 95% CI: -0.0174, -0.0107, p &lt; 0.001). Higher DNAmGrimAge was associated with accelerated decline in grip strength (β = -0.024, 95% CI: -0.033, -0.015, p &lt; 0.001) and decline in walking speed (β = -0.0008, 95% CI: -0.0013, -0.0004, p &lt; 0.001). Higher epigenetic clock biological age estimates, particularly DNAmGrimAge, are retrospectively associated with accelerated frailty-related functional decline across multiple functional domains. Systematic comparison of clock derivations may reveal specific epigenetic patterns underlying age-related functional deterioration.</jats:p>
title: Biological Age Associates with Longitudinal Frailty-Related Functional Decline: The Health and Retirement Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mounting evidence points to the protective role of adult child education in older parents' health, including their risk of ADL and IADL difficulties. Yet, little is known whether this association varies cross-nationally due to contextual differences in intergenerational transfers, family dynamics, and other factors. This study examines the relationship between adult child education and parents’ functional health outcomes across countries, using comparable population-based datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used harmonized data from seven population-based studies accessed through the Gateway to Global Aging Data. Our analytic sample included 88,683 adults 60 years and older from 24 countries. We estimated and meta-analyzed associations between adult child education and respondents’ (parents’) difficulty with basic and instrumental activities of daily living (ADL and IADLs), controlling for respondents’ own education and other socio-demographic characteristics. We also considered heterogeneity across parent and child demographics (e.g. parent gender, child gender).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across all studies, each additional year of education averaged across adult children was associated with a 3% lower risk of difficulty with both ADLs (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.95, 0.98) and IADLs (95% CI: 0.95, 0.98). Statistical heterogeneity appeared to be driven by one study (e.g. I2 = 78.94% when the study was included vs. I2 = 0.04% when excluded). Results suggest limited heterogeneity across demographic subgroups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>“Upward” intergenerational benefits of higher adult child education for parents’ late-life ADL and IADL difficulties appear to be relatively consistent across a range of global settings. Further research is needed to uncover the mechanisms driving these cross-national associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cross-National Comparison of the Association between Adult Child Educational Attainment and Older Parents’ Functional Health

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates whether life-course socioeconomic exposures are similarly associated with accelerated biological aging across racial and ethnic groups, and whether accelerated biological aging predicts health outcomes equivalently across groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data came from the Health and Retirement Study (2016-2022). Accelerated biological age was derived from 22 blood-based biomarkers from the 2016 Venous Blood Study. We used linear regression models with interactions between race/ethnicity and life-course exposures (childhood adversity and adult/midlife socioeconomic status (SES)) to assess group differences in accelerated aging. Linear, multinomial, and logistic regression models with interactions between accelerated biological age and race/ethnicity were used to assess group differences in health outcomes. We examined differences by foreign-born status among Hispanic adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Associations between life-course exposures, accelerated biological aging, and health varied by race/ethnicity. Compared to non-Hispanic White adults, childhood health and adversity were not associated with accelerated biological aging for non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults, and among these groups, higher midlife SES did not decelerate biological aging. The association between accelerated biological age and health outcomes varied by race/ethnicity; accelerated biological age was less predictive among non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults. Among Hispanic adults, foreign-born status was a significant moderator: increased biological age was more strongly linked to morbidity among foreign-born individuals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The processes linking life-course conditions to biological aging, and biological aging to later-life health, do not translate uniformly across racial/ethnic groups. Future research should explore the sources of heterogeneity in life-course exposures and the mechanisms by which biological age translates into health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unequal Embodiment: Racial and Ethnic Heterogeneity in the Predictors and Age-Related Health Outcomes Associated with Accelerated Biological Aging

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Osteosarcopenia is linked to frailty, falls, fractures, and mortality. It may impair intrinsic capacity (IC), with emerging evidence especially pointing to its relationship with cognition capacity. We determined the prevalence and characteristics of persons with possible osteosarcopenia in older adults and examined its association with IC, with a focus on cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>2,291 participants were recruited through a national household survey of older adults in Singapore. Socio-demographic, health, and psychosocial variables were collected using questionnaires and physical assessments at baseline. Possible osteosarcopenia was defined by the concurrent presence of possible osteoporosis and possible sarcopenia. Multilevel mixed‑effects regression models examined the association of possible osteosarcopenia with IC at baseline, and with cognitive function at six months post-baseline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Possible osteosarcopenia, observed among 50.3% of the cohort, was associated with lower IC at baseline, including cognition capacity. Furthermore, baseline possible osteosarcopenia was associated with poor cognitive function at six months post-baseline, particularly among those with loss in cognitive capacity at baseline. This was driven by impaired delayed recall and poor orientation abilities, indicators of both early onset and gradual decline of cognitive impairment. On the other hand, higher education, social networks, resilience, and quality of life were associated with better IC (at baseline) and cognition (at baseline and at six months post-baseline).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Possible osteosarcopenia is prevalent among older adults in Singapore and is associated with loss in intrinsic capacity and cognitive function, highlighting the importance of early intervention in rapidly ageing societies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Possible osteosarcopenia is associated with loss in intrinsic capacity and early cognitive deficits: a longitudinal study of older adults in Singapore

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Whether daytime napping may be a risk factor for dementia, in addition to nighttime sleep disturbances, remains unclear. This study investigated longitudinal associations of napping characteristics with incident dementia among U.S. older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data came from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS). Napping characteristics were self-reported in a sleep module at round 3 (2013), including (1) frequency (non-napper, infrequent, frequent); (2) intention (non-napper, intentional, unintentional); (3) duration (non-napper, ≤30 minutes, &gt;30 minutes). Dementia classification was established at each round using a validated algorithm and possible/probable dementia served as our outcome. We included 995 participants free of possible/probable dementia at round 3 who were followed up to round 13 (2023). Discrete-time complementary log-log models were used for hazard ratio (HR) of incident possible/probable dementia associated with napping characteristics, adjusting for demographic, health, and sleep variables (duration, daytime sleepiness, obstructive sleep apnea risk).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>When compared to non-nappers, frequent nappers had 1.48 times the hazard of developing incident possible/probable dementia (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14, 1.94). Unintentional napping was associated with incident possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.39, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.81). No associations were found for infrequent or intentional napping. Napping ≤30 minutes was associated with possible/probable dementia (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.85), but the association of napping &gt;30 minutes was attenuated with additional adjustment for sleep variables (HR = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.96, 1.69).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daytime napping may be a modifiable risk factor for dementia if supported by further evidence. Future studies with detailed napping characteristics and longer follow-up are needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Napping Characteristics and Incident Dementia: Results From The National Health and Aging Trends Study

                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 240). Compared with the SFGCD group, the DFGCD and DFPCD groups had 1.65-fold and 1.78-fold higher risks of hospitalization, respectively (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.32–2.07 and 95% CI: 1.41–2.24, respectively). The DFPCD group had the highest hazard ratio for mortality (6.62, 95% CI: 5.06–8.97,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). The risk of mortality in the DFGCD group was 5.60-fold higher than that in the SFGCD group (95% CI: 4.39–7.14,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). The DFGCD and DFPCD groups had the shortest median survival time, at 8.0 years. The SFGCD group had the longest median survival time, at 13.0 years (95% CI: 12.74–13.26), while the SFPCD group had a similar median survival time of 12.0 years (95% CI: 11.54–12.46).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights the importance of identifying target population characteristics, optimal timing, and high-risk groups to support the early detection of hospitalization and mortality risks based on frailty and cognitive decline trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: How joint trajectories of frailty and cognitive decline impact hospitalization and mortality: evidence from the Korean longitudinal study of aging 2006–2020

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Well-being in retirement is multidimensional, encompassing physical, mental, social, financial, and spiritual domains. Existing measures are often developed for general populations and may not fully capture retired older adults’ experiences. This study aimed to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Well-being across Individual, Social, Spiritual, and Economic Domains (WISE) Scale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The study involved two phases. First, items were developed from the literature and reviewed by experts for content validity. Second, a cross-sectional survey was conducted with retired older adults in New Brunswick, Canada. After data cleaning, 1,903 responses were randomly divided into two subsamples. Exploratory factor analysis was conducted in Subsample 1 (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 951), followed by confirmatory factor analysis in Subsample 2 (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 952). Reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity were assessed.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Content validity was strong (S-CVI = 0.87). Exploratory factor analysis identified five factors representing physical, mental, social, spiritual, and financial well-being, explaining 51.63% of the variance. Confirmatory factor analysis showed excellent fit (χ²/df = 1.32, RMSEA = 0.02, SRMR = 0.02, CFI = 0.99). Average variance extracted ranged from 0.51 to 0.53, and HTMT values ranged from 0.17 to 0.39, supporting convergent and discriminant validity. Cronbach’s alpha ranged from 0.76 to 0.81, and composite reliability values were consistently above 0.75, supporting internal consistency reliability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The WISE Scale demonstrated promising reliability and construct validity as a multidimensional measure of well-being among retired older adults. The instrument may provide researchers, clinicians, and policymakers with a practical tool for assessing well-being across key domains relevant to retirement and healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Oral intake problems and dysphagia are important clinical issues during rehabilitation in older adults after hip fracture surgery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to determine the proportion of patients with dysphagia based on functional oral intake at acute-care and post-acute care discharge in older adults after hip fracture surgery and to examine its association with prefracture functional and cognitive vulnerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective observational study used multicenter data from the Kitakyushu Liaison Clinical Pathway for Hip Fractures. Patients aged 60 years or older who were admitted to acute-care hospitals for hip fracture and underwent surgery were included. Functional oral intake was classified using dietary information recorded in the pathway, with FOIS levels 1–5 operationally defined as dysphagia. The acute-care discharge analysis included 1725 patients, and the post-acute care discharge analysis included 853 patients. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed using multiple imputation, with complete-case analyses as sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dysphagia was observed in 608 patients (35.2%) at acute-care discharge and in 219 patients (25.7%) at post-acute care discharge. FOIS levels 1–3 were observed in 24 patients (1.4%) and 41 patients (4.8%), respectively. Among the 458 patients with dietary information available at both discharge points, the proportion classified as FOIS-derived levels 1–5 was 36.2% at acute-care discharge and 24.7% at post-acute care discharge, whereas the corresponding proportions for FOIS-derived levels 1–3 were 2.4% and 4.2%, respectively. Older age, dementia, long-term care insurance certification, and lower prefracture Barthel Index (BI) were significantly associated with dysphagia at both acute-care and post-acute care discharge in the main and sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dysphagia based on functional oral intake was frequently observed at both acute-care and post-acute care discharge in older adults after hip fracture surgery. Older age, dementia, long-term care insurance certification, and lower prefracture BI, which may reflect prefracture functional and cognitive vulnerability, were consistently associated with dysphagia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Dysphagia after hip fracture based on functional oral intake and its association with prefracture vulnerability

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sarcopenia is a progressive age-related condition characterized by loss of muscle mass, strength, and function, with particularly high prevalence among nursing home residents and the oldest-old population. Although exercise is a recognized non-pharmacological intervention, existing evidence has largely been generated in selected community-dwelling populations, limiting its applicability to vulnerable older adults in real-world long-term care settings. The SCOPE study (Sarcopenia Care in Oldest-old: a Pragmatic Exercise cluster-randomized controlled trial) evaluates the effectiveness and feasibility of caregiver-led modified Baduanjin, resistance training, and combined exercise interventions for sarcopenia management in nursing home residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pragmatic, cluster-randomized controlled trial aims to recruit 104 residents aged ≥ 75 years with sarcopenia from a large nursing home in Hangzhou, China. Participants will be randomized by residential building into four groups: Modified Baduanjin Group, Resistance Training Group, Combined Exercise Group, and Control Group. The 48-week intervention will be delivered by trained caregivers using video-guided sessions, with phased reduction in specialist supervision. The primary outcome is a composite sarcopenia Z-score integrating handgrip strength, Short Physical Performance Battery, and appendicular skeletal muscle mass index. Secondary outcomes include functional mobility, balance, physical activity and sedentary behaviour, neuromuscular activation, questionnaire-based assessments, and saliva biological markers. Clinical events and care-dependency records will also be collected throughout the intervention and follow-up periods. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, week 12, week 24, week 48, and at 1 and 2 years post-intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The SCOPE study addresses the need for feasible and sustainable exercise interventions for sarcopenia in real-world nursing home settings. By integrating pragmatic caregiver-led delivery, multimodal outcome assessment, and long-term follow-up, this trial aims to inform exercise prescription, implementation feasibility, and potential mechanisms of adaptation in oldest-old nursing home residents. The findings are expected to support the development of scalable exercise intervention frameworks for sarcopenia management in long-term care facilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500107315).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Implementing an exercise intervention for sarcopenia in oldest-old nursing home residents: protocol for a pragmatic cluster-randomized controlled trial (SCOPE Study)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Animal-assisted therapy (AAT) is a promising complementary approach in geriatric rehabilitation, but evidence on feasibility and patient experiences remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This exploratory, mixed-methods, two-arm randomized controlled parallel-group design (RCT) compared dog-assisted exercise therapy (intervention) to standard exercise therapy (active control) in geriatric inpatients during a two-week rehabilitation program. Quantitative data on mobility (TUG), depression (HADS-D) symptoms, motivation (VAS), and satisfaction (VAS)were collected and analysed using descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, group comparisons (unpaired t-test or Mann–Whitney U test), and correlation (Spearman’s ρ). Semi-structured interviews explored patientsexperiences. Data were analyzed separately and integrated using a joint display approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      27 patients participated in the RCT, and 11 in the embedded qualitative study. Quantitative measures showed no clinically meaningful between-group differences in mobility or depressive symptoms: mobility (TUG) (control: Mdn = 16.00, IQR [14.25, 22.50]; intervention: Mdn = 18.00, IQR [13.00, 20.50]); depression (HADS-D) = 0.2 points (95% CI [–3.2, 3.6], SD = 3.05). Motivation and satisfaction were consistently high across conditions. A strong positive correlation was observed between motivation and satisfaction (ρ = 0.65,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < .001). Qualitative results indicated high acceptance and feasibility, enhanced emotional well-being, motivation, social interaction, and engagement, particularly associated with the presence of the therapy dog. Mixed-methods integration indicated high feasibility and acceptability of the intervention. Qualitative findings complemented the quantitative results by demonstrating that the therapy dog enhanced the ward atmosphere and patient engagement, despite the absence of measurable short-term clinical changes.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Limitations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Key limitations include novelty effects, the dog’s visibility across conditions, the influence of prior pet ownership, COVID-19, dropouts, small sample size, the awareness of the presence of the dog at ward for the control group, and a heterogeneity group of conditions. These factors may have impacted the overall outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Animal-assisted exercise therapy is feasible and well accepted in geriatric inpatient care. Its primary benefits appear to be experiential and psychosocial, supporting engagement and rehabilitation participation rather than immediate clinical improvement. Further research should investigate long-term effects and underlying mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study has been registered in the German Clinical Trial Registry with trial ID DRKS00024955 on 22 April 2021 and was approved by the ethics committee (EA4/071/21).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A mixed-methods feasibility study of dog-assisted exercise therapy in geriatric inpatients

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Current fall prevention strategies have been built predominantly on the factors associated with fall occurrence rather than fall-related injury, and the determinants of these two outcomes may be distinct. This study aimed to identify distinct factors associated with past-year fall occurrence (non-fallers vs. fallers) and fall-related injury (non-injurious vs. injurious fallers) in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional, secondary analysis, 9,950 community-dwelling older adults were included (mean age 74.0 years, standard deviation 6.8, 61.6% women). Binomial logistic regression was used to separately identify the associated factors for fall occurrence and fall-related injury, assessing demographics, chronic diseases, functional abilities, and home modifications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Past-year fall occurrence was primarily associated with women (odds ratio (OR) = 1.66, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.19–2.30), drinking (OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.03–1.99), higher number of chronic diseases (OR = 1.3, 95% CI: 1.24–1.36), assistive devices usage (OR = 1.3, 95% CI: 1.19–1.43), and activities of daily living (ADL) limitations (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.04–1.11). In contrast, fall-related injury was associated with younger age (OR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.93–0.99), lower weight (OR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.95–0.996), lower number of assistive devices (OR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.68–0.98), and higher number of ADL limitations (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.01–1.13). Notably, home modifications were not associated with lower odds of either outcome (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       > 0.05).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study highlights distinct differences between the associated factors for past-year fall occurrence and fall-related injury. The inverse association for assistive devices should not be read as evidence that devices protect against injury. Future guidelines should address these outcomes separately.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Distinct factors associated with past-year fall occurrence and fall-related injury among community-dwelling older adults: a cross-sectional analysis

<jats:p>PURPOSE: To define the frequency and annual rate of hypertensive crisis in older patients attending emergency department (ED), the sociodemographic and baseline patient profile, and clinical characteristics and long-term outcome of the hypertensive crisis episode. We also looked for differences between men and women. 

METHODS: This was a retrospective analysis of the multipurpose EDEN cohort, which recruited during 1-week period all patients aged 65 years who visited the ED of 52 Spanish public hospitals covering 19.3% of Spanish population. Demographic, social, baseline and clinical data of the episode of hypertensive crisis were recorded. Estimations of annual incidence were made, in general and through patient age. Outcome consisted of 1-year post-discharge combined adverse event (revisit to ED, hospitalization, or death). Comparison between men and women were performed in unadjusted and adjusted models.
RESULTS: There were 186 cases of hypertensive crises among the 25,557 patients included in the EDEN cohort. The relative frequency of hypertensive crisis was 0.73% of ED visits (95%CI 0.63-0.84), with 0.56% (0.44-0.72) in men and 0.87% (0.73-1.04) in women (OR for men 0.64, 0.47-0.87), and annual rate of hypertensive crisis in Spanish older population was 429 cases per 100.000 inhabitants (95%CI 371-493), with 341 (267-436) in men and 493 (413-590) in women (OR for men 0.69, 0.51-0.94). Patients with hypertensive crisis had better baseline health status than the rest of the older patients attending the ED, with cardiovascular comorbidity being frequent (previously known hypertension in 88.2%) and with 22% having additional acute diagnoses on top of the hypertensive crisis. Hospitalization was needed in 7.5% of cases (0.5% in intensive care unit) and in-hospital mortality was observed in 2 cases (1.1%). Combined adverse events 1 year after discharge accounted for 57.9% of patients, with 65.6% in men and 52.5% in women (adjusted HR 1.61, 1.01-2.57). 

CONCLUSIONS: Hypertensive crises are more frequent in older women than men and they present a worse profile at baseline and higher severity than men. Nonetheless, men with hypertensive crisis may have a worse long-term prognosis compared to women, highlighting the need for targeted post-discharge monitoring strategies in this subgroup.</jats:p>
title: Hypertensive crisis in the elderly: epidemiological, clinical and outcome: EDEN-47 study
